newsitem.title: UK: United Utils on track but profits disappoint.
newsitem.headline: United Utils on track but profits disappoint.

text.p: Britain's United Utilities on Thursday disappointed the stock market with annual profits below expectations but said the integration of its water and electricity business was firmly on track.

"The group produced a solid business performance... delivering its promises in respect of the Norweb acquisition. But the most significant achievement has been laying sound foundations for future growth," it said in a statement.

United's pre-tax, pre-exceptionals profit for the year to March 31 were 444 million pounds ($726.5 million), up from 389.2 million, but below expectations of 458-475 million. The dividend rose to 37.2 pence per shares from 32.66.
But United had to take an 83 million pound charge for losses on operations in Bangkok and suffered a loss on disposals of 77.1 million.
"The results are slightly disappointing," one marketmaker said as United's shares fell to 690 pence. They then recovered to be down nine pence at 698.5 pence by 1020 GMT.

Chief executive Brian Staples said the exceptional charge, announced in February and relating to problems over a contract to build sewage works and networks in Bangkok, was "a serious disappointment".
But he added the company was on track to deliver the financial benefits promised when it was formed as North West Water took over regional electricity company (Rec) Norweb in 1995.
"This year I think the figure is 104 million pounds (target for benefits) and it's effectively secured by the actions we took last year...all on course," he told Reuters.
United said it was confident its goal of 474 million of cumulative savings by March 2000 would be met.
"We are now a focused utility service provider following the substantial completion of our disposal programme, on time and ahead of our target," chairman Sir Desmond Pitcher said in a statement.
Vertex, the company's business services unit, had had a superb first year, Staples said. "We are extremely pleased with it," he added.
The unit combines business services of the group's operations and last month formed a joint venture for outsourcing with Northern Ireland Electricity.
Staples said more deals along those lines could be expected.
United, like other utilities, said it disagreed with the principle of a one-off tax on "excess profits" of privatised utilities planned by the new Labour government.
But it said any such levy should be a one-off charge only on its regulated businesses and "at a reasonable level".
Staples said he would be surprised if any eventual tax were able to be challenged legally as some companies have suggested.
"I think our reaction to it will be to look at it in terms of fairness and the way that it's applied".
He added that the company hoped the government would listen to its calls for leniency because it had already shared benefits with customers.
The government has also proposed a 10-point plan with mandatory targets for leakage reduction for water companies, aimed at tackling the problems of the country's worst drought for 200 years.

Staples said United could fulfil the plan because although 24 percent of its supplies were leaking out of pipes, it had been singled out by industry regulator Ofwat for making "excellent progress" in this area.
United should not have to impose any restrictions on none-essential water use, such as bans on garden hoses, this summer, he added. ($ = 0.611 British Pounds)
